Rykiel, Jr.' (Center for Biosystems Modelling, Texas A&M University); Crossref omits the 'Jr.'. The issue number (3) is from Crossref; the title page shows only 'Ecological Modelling 90 (1996) 229-244'. Received 7 March 1995, accepted 25 August 1995. The brief's description matches this real work.

claims.paper: rewrite (brief Phase 5): what validation can mean for an ecological model
claims.claim: Validation means a model is acceptable for its intended use because it meets specified performance requirements, not that it is true
claims.source_value: as claimed: validation is 'a demonstration that a model within its domain of applicability possesses a satisfactory range of accuracy consistent with the intended application', indicating acceptability for use, 'not that it embodies any absolute truth, nor even that it is the best model available' (p. 233)
claims.quote: a model is acceptable for its intended use because it meets specified performance requirements

claims.paper: rewrite (brief Phase 5): what validation cannot mean
claims.claim: Matching observations does not show that a model's mechanisms are correct; the theoretical component cannot be validated
claims.source_value: as claimed: the operational and data components can be validated, the theoretical cannot (abstract); good predictions do not require a mechanistically correct model (p. 234); predicting independent data does not make the model an accurate cause-and-effect representation (p. 239); testing cannot logically prove the mechanisms complete and correct (p. 242)
claims.quote: The operational and data components can be validated; the theoretical component cannot.
claims.note: p. 234: 'in general, it is not true that good predictions can only be obtained from a model that is mechanistically correct'. p. 242: such testing 'cannot logically prove that the mechanisms contained in the model are scientifically complete and correct'.

claims.paper: rewrite (brief Phase 5): what a validation claim must state
claims.claim: A claim of validation needs the model's purpose, the performance criteria and the context stated; without them a model cannot be validated
claims.source_value: as claimed: the modeller must specify (1) purpose, (2) criteria for acceptability, (3) the context of intended operation; the latter two are seldom specified, and without them a model cannot be validated; the most common problem is failure to state the criteria
claims.quote: the modeller must specify three things: (1) the purpose of the model

claims.paper: rewrite (brief Phase 5): validation is bound to its context
claims.claim: Validation holds only within the stated context and domain; a changed context needs re-validation
claims.source_value: as claimed: a model is validated within a specific context that is part of the certification; if the context changes the model must be re-validated, without invalidating it for the original context; qualification tests extend or restrict the domain (§3.5)
claims.quote: If the context changes, the model must be re-validated

claims.paper: rewrite (brief Phase 5): validation is not always required
claims.claim: Validation is not required of every model; for exploratory or theory-building models it may be unnecessary
claims.source_value: as claimed: exploration of model behaviour without validation is legitimate and reportable; when the purpose is to describe or systematize knowledge or develop theory, 'validation is unnecessary and irrelevant'
claims.quote: to develop theory, validation is unnecessary and irrelevant

claims.paper: rewrite (suggested, not in the brief): a quantitative validation convention
claims.claim: Rykiel proposed an operational validation convention
claims.source_value: an initial proposal: for the most important variables of dynamic models, outputs within the 95 % confidence interval 75 % of the time; offered as an arbitrary convention, like P = 0.05
claims.quote: model outputs fall within the 95% confidence interval 75% of the time
